units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Herbs as raw materials and Indian systems of medicine

Every herbal medicine starts as a plant growing in a field or a forest. The quality of the finished product can never be better than the quality of the plant that went into it. This unit follows the herb from its source, through cultivation, collection and processing, to the point where it is ready for the factory. The second half introduces the Indian systems of medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy) and the preparation and standardisation of the classical Ayurvedic dosage forms: Asava and Arishta, Gutika, Churna, Lehya and Bhasma.

## 1.1 Basic definitions

The words below are used in the WHO guidelines on herbal medicines and in most textbooks. Learn the difference between them, because a definition question is a common 5-mark or 2-mark item.

| Term | Meaning (in plain words) | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Herb** | Crude plant material — leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, stems, wood, bark, roots, rhizomes or other parts — whole, cut or powdered | Dried senna leaf, ginger rhizome |
| **Herbal material** | Herbs plus other plant products such as fresh juices, gums, fixed oils, volatile oils, resins and dry powders of herbs, sometimes processed by local methods (steaming, roasting, baking with honey) | Aloe juice, acacia gum, clove oil |
| **Herbal preparation** (herbal drug preparation) | Herbal material processed further by extraction, distillation, expression, fractionation, purification, concentration or fermentation; the starting point of finished products | Powders, tinctures, dry extracts, fatty oils, expressed juices |
| **Finished herbal product** (herbal medicinal product) | Herbal preparation(s) made into a dosage form ready for the patient; may contain excipients | Tablets of ashwagandha extract, Triphala churna, cough syrup with tulsi |
| **Herbal medicine** | The overall group: herbs, herbal materials, herbal preparations and finished herbal products whose active ingredients are plant parts or plant materials | — |

Two more terms appear in exam questions:

- **Phytopharmaceutical**: a purified and standardised fraction of a plant extract with defined marker compounds, studied like a modern drug.
- **Marker compound**: a chemically defined constituent used to check identity and quality, whether or not it is the active compound (for example, withaferin A in ashwagandha, curcumin in turmeric).

A product that contains an isolated, chemically pure constituent (morphine, digoxin, quinine) is **not** a herbal medicine; it is a drug of natural origin.

## 1.2 Sources of herbs

| Source | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wild collection** (forests, waste lands) | Cheap, no farming cost, plants grow in their natural habitat | Variable quality, wrong species collected, adulteration, over-harvesting and loss of species, no records of origin, contamination |
| **Cultivation** (farms, plantations) | Known species and variety, uniform quality, planned harvest, records kept, GAP possible, pests controlled, protects wild stock | Cost of land and labour, some plants give less active content in cultivation, needs know-how |
| **Plant tissue culture** | Year-round production, no soil or climate dependence, free from pests | Expensive; few products made commercially this way |
| **Imports** | Plants not grown in India | Price, quality and supply depend on other countries |

In India most medicinal plants used by industry are still collected from the wild. The National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) supports cultivation and conservation so that pressure on wild plants falls.

Plants sourced for industry are grouped as:

- **Cultivated drugs**: ginger, turmeric, senna, isabgol, ashwagandha, aloe, mentha, opium poppy (licensed).
- **Wild-collected drugs**: many forest roots and barks, for example *Rauwolfia*, kutki, jatamansi, guggul.
- **Endangered or restricted drugs**: species whose collection is controlled to prevent extinction; using cultivated material is preferred.

## 1.3 Selection, identification and authentication of herbal materials

### Selection

The right plant must be chosen for a product. Factors are:

1. **Correct species and plant part** as given in the official text or formula (root, not stem; seed, not leaf).
2. **Chemotype or variety** — some varieties of the same species have far more active constituent than others.
3. **Geographical source, season and time of collection** — content changes with age, season and even time of day (for example, volatile oils are highest before flowering in many herbs).
4. **Freedom from contamination** — pesticides, heavy metals, microbes, aflatoxins.
5. **Sustainable supply** and legal permission to collect.

### Identification and authentication

Authentication means proving that the material really is the plant claimed and is of acceptable quality. Mistakes happen because of similar-looking plants, the same vernacular name used for different plants, and deliberate substitution.

| Method | What is checked |
| --- | --- |
| **Taxonomic identity** | Voucher specimen compared with herbarium sheet; identification by a botanist; a voucher kept with the batch record |
| **Macroscopy / organoleptic** | Shape, size, colour, surface, fracture, odour, taste |
| **Microscopy** | Tissues and cell contents: trichomes, stomata, calcium oxalate crystals, starch grains, vessels, fibres; quantitative microscopy (stomatal index, palisade ratio, vein-islet number) |
| **Physicochemical** | Ash values, extractive values, moisture, swelling index, foaming index, bitterness value |
| **Chemical** | Identification tests for constituent groups; TLC or HPTLC fingerprint against a reference; marker assay by HPLC |
| **DNA-based methods** | DNA barcoding, RAPD, AFLP — used when plant parts look alike or the material is powdered |

Authentication is done for every batch on receipt, and the material stays in **quarantine** until it passes.

## 1.4 Processing of herbal raw material

After harvest, the plant passes through a series of steps that decide its final quality.

```text
Harvest (right part, right stage, right season, dry weather)
      │
      ▼
Primary processing on the farm
  cleaning → washing (only if allowed) → removal of foreign matter
      │
      ▼
Drying (sun, shade, or artificial dryer at controlled temperature)
      │
      ▼
Garbling (sorting out stems, other plant parts, stones, insects)
      │
      ▼
Cutting / size reduction (if specified)
      │
      ▼
Packing (clean, dry, labelled containers)  →  Storage (cool, dry, pest-free)
      │
      ▼
Transport to manufacturer  →  quarantine  →  testing  →  release
```

Points to explain in an answer:

- **Collection**: by hand or machine; only the specified part; dust and soil avoided; damaged or diseased plants rejected; collectors trained.
- **Drying**: the most important step. It stops enzyme action and microbial growth. Leaves and flowers are dried in shade or at low temperature to save colour and volatile oil; roots and barks can take higher temperatures. Moisture is brought low enough to prevent mould. Some drugs need special treatment — for example, *fermentation* (curing) of vanilla pods and *sweating* of some barks to develop aroma or colour.
- **Garbling**: removing unwanted matter by hand or by sieving and winnowing.
- **Special processing**: blanching, peeling (ginger), boiling (turmeric is boiled before drying), slicing, and in Ayurveda *shodhana* (purification) of toxic drugs such as *Strychnos* (kupilu) or *Aconitum* (vatsanabha) before use.
- **Packing and storage**: in clean containers that keep out moisture, light and pests; labelled with name, part, source, batch and date; stored away from finished products.

## 1.5 Biodynamic agriculture

Biodynamic agriculture is a form of organic farming based on the lectures given by **Rudolf Steiner** in 1924. It treats the farm as one self-sustaining living organism in which soil, plants, animals and the farmer are linked.

Main features:

1. **No synthetic fertilisers or pesticides**; fertility comes from compost and farm manure.
2. **Biodynamic preparations** added in very small amounts to soil, compost and crops:
   - **Preparation 500 (horn manure)**: cow dung packed in a cow horn and buried in soil over winter; stirred in water and sprayed on soil to improve soil structure and root growth.
   - **Preparation 501 (horn silica)**: finely ground quartz packed in a horn and buried over summer; sprayed on leaves to improve light use and ripening.
   - **Compost preparations 502–507**: made from yarrow, chamomile, stinging nettle, oak bark, dandelion and valerian; added to the compost heap.
3. **Sowing calendar**: sowing, cultivation and harvest are timed according to the positions of the moon and planets.
4. Crop rotation, mixed cropping, green manure and integration of livestock.

Value for medicinal plants: high-quality, residue-free raw material and better soil health. The scientific basis of some practices (such as the planetary calendar) is not proven, and an answer may say so.

## 1.6 Good agricultural practices (GAP / GACP)

**Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP)** are guidelines that make sure medicinal plants are grown and collected in a way that gives safe, good-quality and consistent raw material. WHO published GACP guidelines for medicinal plants, and in India the National Medicinal Plants Board has issued GACP guidelines based on them.

| Area | What GACP asks for |
| --- | --- |
| **Identity of plant** | Correct botanical identity of seeds and planting material; voucher specimens kept |
| **Site selection** | Soil and water free from heavy metals, pesticide residues and sewage; history of the land known; suitable climate |
| **Seeds and propagation material** | Certified, disease-free, traceable to source |
| **Cultivation** | Proper spacing, irrigation with clean water, fertilisers (preferably organic) applied only as needed, crop rotation |
| **Crop protection** | Minimum use of pesticides; only approved ones, in permitted amounts; integrated pest management preferred |
| **Harvest** | Correct season, stage and time; dry weather; clean tools; damaged plants removed |
| **Primary processing** | Prompt washing/drying; clean drying areas; protection from animals, birds and insects |
| **Packing, storage, transport** | Clean, labelled containers; dry, ventilated store; no mixing with other materials |
| **Personnel** | Trained, healthy workers with protective clothing; hygiene facilities |
| **Documentation** | Records of every step (seed, field, inputs, harvest, processing) so each batch can be traced back |
| **Collection from the wild** | Permission to collect; sustainable amounts; species not endangered; collectors trained |

### Organic farming

Organic farming grows crops **without synthetic fertilisers, synthetic pesticides, growth regulators or genetically modified organisms**. Fertility is maintained by compost, farmyard manure, vermicompost, green manure, crop rotation and biofertilisers (*Rhizobium*, *Azotobacter*, phosphate-solubilising bacteria, mycorrhiza). Pests are managed by biological and cultural means.

Why it matters for herbal drugs: no pesticide residue in the final product, better acceptance in export markets, and long-term soil health. Organic produce is certified by accredited bodies; in India the **National Programme for Organic Production (NPOP)** provides the certification framework.

## 1.7 Pests and pest management in medicinal plants

Pests that damage medicinal plants include insects (aphids, caterpillars, beetles, whiteflies), mites, nematodes, fungi (rusts, wilts, root rot, mildews), bacteria, viruses, weeds, rodents and birds. Stored drugs are attacked by beetles, moths, mites and moulds.

**Pest management** methods:

| Method | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Cultural | Crop rotation, clean seed, proper spacing, removal of infected plants, correct sowing time, trap crops |
| Mechanical / physical | Hand picking, traps (light traps, pheromone traps, sticky traps), barriers, heat or cold treatment of stored drugs |
| Biological | Natural enemies — predators (ladybird beetle against aphids), parasitoids (*Trichogramma*), microbial agents |
| Chemical | Synthetic pesticides — used only when needed and within permitted limits, because residues enter the drug |
| **Integrated pest management (IPM)** | A planned combination of the above that keeps pests below damaging levels with the least chemical use |

### Biopesticides and bioinsecticides

Biopesticides are pest-control agents from living organisms or natural products. They are specific, break down quickly and leave little residue, which makes them the preferred choice for medicinal crops.

| Group | Source and active principle | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Botanical insecticides | Neem (*Azadirachta indica*, Meliaceae) seed — **azadirachtin**: antifeedant, repellent and growth regulator | Wide range of insects |
| | Pyrethrum (*Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium*, Asteraceae) flowers — **pyrethrins** | Quick knock-down of flying insects |
| | Derris and *Lonchocarpus* roots — **rotenone** | Insecticide, fish poison |
| | Tobacco — **nicotine** | Sucking insects (old use) |
| Microbial insecticides | ***Bacillus thuringiensis*** — protein crystal toxic to caterpillar gut | Lepidopteran larvae |
| | Fungi: *Beauveria bassiana*, *Metarhizium anisopliae* | Insects, termites |
| | Nuclear polyhedrosis viruses (NPV) | *Helicoverpa*, *Spodoptera* larvae |
| Biofungicides | *Trichoderma viride*, *T. harzianum*; *Pseudomonas fluorescens* | Soil-borne fungal diseases, seed treatment |
| Pheromones | Sex pheromone traps | Monitoring and mass trapping |

## 1.8 Indian systems of medicine — basic principles

India officially recognises Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, under the Ministry of AYUSH. The syllabus covers four of them.

### Ayurveda

"Ayurveda" means the science (*veda*) of life (*ayu*). Its main texts are the *Charaka Samhita* (medicine), *Sushruta Samhita* (surgery) and *Ashtanga Hridaya*.

| Principle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Panchamahabhuta** | Everything, including the body and drugs, is made of five elements: *prithvi* (earth), *jala* (water), *agni/tejas* (fire), *vayu* (air) and *akasha* (space) |
| **Tridosha** | Three functional forces: **vata** (air + space; movement, nerve action), **pitta** (fire + water; digestion, metabolism, heat), **kapha** (earth + water; structure, lubrication, stability). Health = balance of the three; disease = imbalance |
| **Sapta dhatu** | Seven tissues: rasa (plasma), rakta (blood), mamsa (muscle), meda (fat), asthi (bone), majja (marrow), shukra (reproductive tissue) |
| **Mala** | Waste products: faeces, urine, sweat |
| **Agni** | Digestive and metabolic fire; weak agni produces *ama* (undigested toxic matter) |
| **Prakriti** | Individual constitution decided at conception by the dominant dosha |
| **Drug action** | Explained by *rasa* (taste — six tastes), *guna* (properties), *virya* (potency — hot or cold), *vipaka* (post-digestive effect) and *prabhava* (special action) |

Treatment includes *shodhana* (purification, such as Panchakarma), *shamana* (palliation with medicines), diet (*pathya*) and lifestyle, and *rasayana* (rejuvenation).

### Siddha

Siddha is practised mainly in Tamil Nadu and is traditionally linked to the Siddhars, especially **Agastya**.

- Also accepts five elements and **three humours** — *vatham*, *pitham*, *kapham* — similar to the doshas.
- Describes the body in terms of **96 basic principles (thathuvas)**.
- Diagnosis relies heavily on **eight methods (envagai thervu)**, including pulse (*naadi*), tongue, colour, voice, eyes, touch, urine and stools.
- Makes great use of **metals and minerals** (*parpam*, *chendooram*) and of herbs, besides diet and yoga.

### Unani

Unani (Unani-Tibb) comes from Greek medicine (Hippocrates, Galen), developed by Arab and Persian physicians such as **Ibn Sina** (Avicenna), and came to India with the Arabs and Persians.

- **Four humours (akhlat)**: *dam* (blood), *balgham* (phlegm), *safra* (yellow bile), *sauda* (black bile). Health is their balance.
- **Temperament (mizaj)**: hot, cold, moist, dry and their combinations, for persons and drugs.
- **Six essentials (asbab-e-sitta zarooriya)** for health: air, food and drink, bodily movement and rest, mental movement and rest, sleep and wakefulness, retention and evacuation.
- **Quwwat-e-mudabbira-e-badan** — the body's own power of self-healing.
- Treatment: regimental therapy (*ilaj bil tadbeer* — cupping, massage, exercise), diet therapy (*ilaj bil ghiza*), pharmacotherapy (*ilaj bil dawa*) and surgery.

### Homoeopathy

Founded by **Samuel Hahnemann** (Germany, late 18th century).

| Principle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Law of similars** (*similia similibus curentur*) | A substance that produces symptoms in a healthy person can cure similar symptoms in a sick person |
| **Drug proving** | Drugs are tested on healthy volunteers to record the symptoms they produce |
| **Single remedy** | One medicine at a time |
| **Minimum dose** | The smallest amount that can produce a cure |
| **Potentisation (dynamisation)** | Serial dilution with vigorous shaking (succussion) or grinding with lactose (trituration); decimal (X) and centesimal (C) scales |
| **Individualisation** | The whole person, not just the disease, is treated |

Starting materials are **mother tinctures** (Ø) made mostly from plants, and also from minerals and animal products.

## 1.9 Preparation and standardisation of Ayurvedic formulations

The official Ayurvedic texts list hundreds of classical formulations. Their preparation is described in the *Ayurvedic Formulary of India* (AFI), and their quality standards in the *Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India* (API).

### Asava and Arishta (fermented liquid preparations)

Both are liquid preparations in which **self-produced alcohol**, produced by fermentation of sugar, extracts the active constituents and also preserves the product.

| Point | Asava | Arishta |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How the herbs are used | Raw drugs or their juices/powders added **without boiling** (cold process) | A **decoction** (*kwatha*) of the drugs is made first, then fermented (hot process) |
| Examples | Drakshasava, Kumaryasava, Kanakasava, Lohasava | Dashamularishta, Ashokarishta, Arjunarishta, Abhayarishta |

**General method**

1. Prepare the decoction (Arishta) or the cold liquid (Asava) as given in the formula; strain.
2. Dissolve the sweetening agent — **jaggery, sugar or honey** — which supplies the sugar for fermentation.
3. Add the **fermentation initiator**, traditionally the flowers of **dhataki (*Woodfordia fruticosa*)**, which carry natural yeasts, and the powdered *prakshepa dravya* (flavouring and aromatic drugs).
4. Fill into a clean, fumigated wooden vat or earthen/glazed vessel, leaving some space; seal the mouth.
5. Keep in a warm, quiet place for the fermentation period stated in the text (usually about a month). Fermentation is complete when bubbling stops, a lit match held near the mouth no longer goes out, and the liquid has a characteristic aromatic odour and turns clear.
6. Decant, filter, allow to settle, and fill into bottles. The product keeps well because of the alcohol.

**Standardisation of Asava/Arishta**

- Organoleptic characters: colour, odour, taste, clarity.
- pH, specific gravity, total solids.
- **Alcohol content** (self-produced) by distillation — must be within the monograph's limits; no added alcohol.
- Methanol must be absent (safety).
- Reducing and non-reducing sugars.
- TLC/HPTLC fingerprint for identity of ingredients.
- Microbial limits, heavy metals and pesticide residues.

### Gutika (vati) — pills and tablets

Gutika are pills or tablets made from fine powders of drugs bound with a liquid (water, juice, decoction, honey, jaggery or guggul). Examples: Chandraprabha vati, Sanjivani vati, Arogyavardhini vati, Lasunadi vati.

**Method**: powder and sieve the drugs → triturate with the binding liquid (*bhavana*) as directed → roll into pills of the prescribed weight by hand or pill machine, or compress as tablets → dry in shade or a low-temperature dryer → pack.

**Standardisation**: description, uniformity of weight, hardness, disintegration time, moisture (loss on drying), ash values, extractive values, TLC fingerprint, microbial limits, heavy metals.

### Churna — fine powders

Churna is a fine powder of one or more drugs, dried and finely sieved, and mixed uniformly. Examples: Triphala churna, Sitopaladi churna, Hingvashtaka churna, Avipattikar churna.

**Method**: clean and dry the ingredients → powder separately → pass through a fine sieve (the formulary specifies the fineness) → mix in the proportions given → store in airtight containers. Salts and sugar, where included, are powdered and added at the end.

**Standardisation**: colour, odour, taste; particle size (sieve test); loss on drying; total ash and acid-insoluble ash; water- and alcohol-soluble extractives; pH of an aqueous solution; bulk density; microscopy of each ingredient (useful for detecting omission or substitution); TLC; microbial load, aflatoxins, heavy metals.

Churnas absorb moisture and grow mould, so moisture control and good packing are critical.

### Lehya (avaleha) — semisolid preparations

Lehya are semisolid, jam-like preparations of drugs cooked with **jaggery, sugar or sugar candy**, usually with ghee or oil and finished with honey. Examples: **Chyawanprash**, Agastya haritaki rasayana, Kushmanda avaleha.

**Method**: prepare the decoction or juice → dissolve jaggery/sugar and filter → heat on a mild fire with constant stirring until the right consistency (*paka*) is reached — the mass sinks in water without spreading, or forms a thread between two fingers → add the fine powders and ghee/oil, mix thoroughly → cool and add honey when lukewarm → store in clean, dry, wide-mouthed containers.

**Standardisation**: description, consistency, moisture, total ash, acid-insoluble ash, pH, reducing and non-reducing sugars, fat content where ghee is used, TLC, microbial limits and heavy metals.

### Bhasma — calcined metallic and mineral preparations

Bhasma are fine powders obtained by repeated incineration of purified metals, minerals or animal products (shells, pearls) with herbal juices. Examples: Swarna (gold) bhasma, Abhraka (mica) bhasma, Lauha (iron) bhasma, Yashada (zinc) bhasma, Shankha (conch shell) bhasma, Praval (coral) bhasma.

```text
Raw metal/mineral
   │ Shodhana (purification): heating and quenching in
   │ liquids such as oil, buttermilk, cow's urine, decoctions
   ▼
Purified material
   │ Bhavana (trituration with herbal juices), made into small cakes (chakrika), dried
   ▼
Marana (incineration): cakes sealed in earthen saucers (sarava samputa),
heated in a pit with cow-dung cakes ("puta"); repeated many times
   ▼
Fine, lustreless, tasteless powder = Bhasma
```

**Classical tests for a properly made bhasma**

| Test | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| **Rekhapurnatva** | Powder enters and fills the lines of the fingertips (very fine) |
| **Varitara** | A small amount floats on still water (fineness, lightness) |
| **Nishchandratva** | No metallic lustre seen in bright light |
| **Nirutthatva / Apunarbhava** | Does not revert to the metal when heated with specified substances |
| **Nirdhuma** | No fumes on heating |
| Taste and colour | Tasteless (no metallic taste); characteristic colour |

**Modern standardisation**: particle size, X-ray diffraction (chemical form of the metal), scanning electron microscopy, elemental analysis (atomic absorption, ICP), loss on drying, acid-insoluble ash, and safety studies. Bhasmas contain metals by design, so their safety depends entirely on correct processing.

## Remember

- Herb → herbal material → herbal preparation → finished herbal product: learn the four definitions with examples.
- Wild collection is cheap but variable and harmful to species; cultivation gives uniform, traceable material.
- Authentication: voucher specimen, macroscopy, microscopy, physicochemical values, chemical tests, TLC/HPTLC fingerprint, DNA methods; quarantine until released.
- Drying is the key processing step; garbling removes foreign matter.
- Biodynamic farming: Rudolf Steiner; preparations 500 (horn manure), 501 (horn silica), 502–507 (compost herbs); sowing calendar.
- GACP covers identity, site, seed, cultivation, pesticides, harvest, processing, storage, personnel and documentation.
- Biopesticides: azadirachtin (neem), pyrethrins, rotenone, *Bacillus thuringiensis*, *Beauveria*, *Trichoderma*, NPV.
- Ayurveda: panchamahabhuta, tridosha (vata, pitta, kapha), sapta dhatu, rasa–guna–virya–vipaka–prabhava.
- Siddha: three humours, 96 thathuvas, eight-fold diagnosis, metals and minerals. Unani: four humours, mizaj, six essentials. Homoeopathy: similia, proving, single remedy, minimum dose, potentisation.
- Asava = cold, Arishta = decoction; both ferment with jaggery/sugar and dhataki flowers to self-produced alcohol.
- Churna = fine powder; Gutika = pills; Lehya = jam with jaggery, ghee, honey (Chyawanprash); Bhasma = shodhana → bhavana → marana, tested by rekhapurnatva, varitara, nishchandratva, apunarbhava.

# Unit 2: Nutraceuticals and herb–drug, herb–food interactions

Many people now take herbs not as medicines for a disease but as foods and supplements to stay healthy. This unit explains what nutraceuticals are, what kinds of products are on the market and how they help in common diseases. It then covers ten herbs used as health foods, and finally the interactions of herbs with modern drugs and foods — a topic that matters to every pharmacist because patients rarely tell their doctor that they take herbal supplements.

## 2.1 Nutraceuticals — general aspects

The word **nutraceutical** joins "nutrition" and "pharmaceutical". It was coined by Stephen DeFelice in 1989. A nutraceutical is **a food, or part of a food, that provides medical or health benefits, including the prevention or treatment of disease**, beyond basic nutrition.

Related terms:

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dietary supplement** | Product taken by mouth that adds a dietary ingredient (vitamin, mineral, herb, amino acid) to the diet; sold as tablets, capsules, powders | Multivitamin tablet, ginseng capsule |
| **Functional food** | An ordinary-looking food that has been fortified or is naturally rich in a health-promoting component | Probiotic yoghurt, omega-3 eggs, iodised salt |
| **Medical food** | Food made for the dietary management of a disease under medical supervision | Formulas for phenylketonuria |
| **Phytonutrient** | Health-promoting non-nutrient compound from plants | Lycopene, resveratrol, sulforaphane |

In India, nutraceuticals and health supplements are regulated as **foods** by the **Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)** under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and its regulations for health supplements and nutraceuticals — not as drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. They may not claim to cure a disease.

### Classification of nutraceuticals

1. **By source**: plant (lycopene, curcumin, flavonoids), animal (fish oil omega-3, chitosan, glucosamine, collagen), microbial (probiotics such as *Lactobacillus*, spirulina, yeast products), minerals.
2. **By chemical nature**: polyphenols (flavonoids, anthocyanins, catechins), carotenoids (beta-carotene, lycopene, lutein), dietary fibre (inulin, psyllium, beta-glucan), fatty acids (omega-3: EPA, DHA, alpha-linolenic acid), phytosterols, glucosinolates, peptides and amino acids, vitamins and minerals.
3. **By product type**:
   - **Dietary supplements** — tablets, capsules, powders, liquids.
   - **Functional foods** — fortified or enriched foods, probiotic foods, prebiotic foods.
   - **Herbal/botanical products** — ginseng, ashwagandha, garlic, ginkgo.
   - **Sports and energy products**, **weight-management products**, **infant and elderly nutrition**.

### Probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics

- **Probiotics**: live microorganisms that, when taken in adequate amounts, give a health benefit (*Lactobacillus*, *Bifidobacterium*, *Saccharomyces boulardii*).
- **Prebiotics**: non-digestible food components that selectively feed beneficial gut bacteria (inulin from chicory, fructo-oligosaccharides, galacto-oligosaccharides).
- **Synbiotics**: a probiotic and a prebiotic combined in one product.

## 2.2 Market, growth and scope

The nutraceutical market in India and worldwide has grown fast and continues to grow. Reasons for growth:

- Rising awareness of health, diet and preventive care.
- Increase in lifestyle diseases — diabetes, obesity, heart disease, hypertension.
- Ageing population and higher spending on wellness.
- Belief that natural products are safe; growing interest in Ayurveda and traditional foods.
- Easy access through pharmacies, supermarkets and online sales; sports and fitness culture.
- India's strengths: rich biodiversity, a long tradition of herbs in food (turmeric, amla, ginger), and a strong manufacturing base.

Challenges: unproven health claims, poor quality control, adulteration, lack of clinical evidence for many products, unclear regulation in the past, and interactions with medicines.

Scope for the pharmacist: formulation and stability of nutraceuticals, quality control and standardisation, regulatory documentation, research on evidence, and counselling patients on safe use.

## 2.3 Health benefits and role in diseases

| Condition | Nutraceuticals used | How they are thought to act |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Diabetes** | Fenugreek seed, bitter gourd, cinnamon, gymnema, dietary fibre (psyllium, guar gum), chromium, alpha-lipoic acid | Slow carbohydrate absorption (fibre), improve insulin sensitivity, increase insulin secretion, reduce oxidative stress |
| **Cardiovascular disease** | Omega-3 fatty acids, garlic, phytosterols, soluble fibre (oat beta-glucan, psyllium), soy protein, flavonoids (cocoa, tea), coenzyme Q10, red yeast rice | Lower LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, lower blood pressure, reduce platelet aggregation, antioxidant protection of LDL |
| **Cancer** (prevention, supportive) | Lycopene (tomato), curcumin, green tea catechins (EGCG), sulforaphane (broccoli), resveratrol, selenium, dietary fibre | Antioxidant action, induce detoxifying enzymes, block cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, anti-inflammatory |
| **Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)** | Probiotics, soluble fibre (psyllium), peppermint oil, ginger | Restore gut flora, normalise bowel movement, relax smooth muscle (peppermint), reduce gas and pain |
| **Other gastrointestinal diseases** — constipation, diarrhoea, ulcers, inflammatory bowel disease | Fibre (isabgol), probiotics, prebiotics (inulin), liquorice (deglycyrrhizinised), aloe, zinc | Bulk and softening of stool, protection of mucosa, competition with harmful bacteria, short-chain fatty acids for colon cells |

Answers in this topic should name the nutraceutical, its key constituent and its mechanism, and add that nutraceuticals **support** but do not replace prescribed treatment.

## 2.4 Herbs as health foods

For each herb learn: biological source with family, important constituents, health-food uses and any caution.

### Alfalfa

- **Source**: leaves and herb of *Medicago sativa*, family Fabaceae (Leguminosae).
- **Constituents**: proteins, vitamins (A, C, E, K and B group), minerals (calcium, iron, magnesium), chlorophyll, saponins, isoflavones and coumestans (coumestrol, a phytoestrogen), fibre.
- **Uses**: nutritive tonic, cholesterol lowering (saponins bind cholesterol), source of vitamin K, used in sprouts and tablets.
- **Caution**: seeds and sprouts contain **L-canavanine**, linked to lupus-like reactions; vitamin K content can reduce the effect of warfarin.

### Chicory

- **Source**: roots and leaves of *Cichorium intybus*, family Asteraceae.
- **Constituents**: **inulin** (a fructan, a major part of the dried root), sesquiterpene lactones (bitter: lactucin, lactucopicrin), coumarins, phenolic acids (chicoric acid).
- **Uses**: roasted root as a **coffee substitute or additive**; inulin as a **prebiotic** and dietary fibre; mild laxative, appetiser, liver tonic; source of inulin for food industry.
- **Caution**: allergy in people sensitive to the Asteraceae family.

### Ginger

- **Source**: rhizome of *Zingiber officinale*, family Zingiberaceae.
- **Constituents**: volatile oil (zingiberene, bisabolene), pungent principles **gingerols** (fresh) and **shogaols** (formed on drying and heating), zingerone, starch.
- **Uses**: anti-nausea (motion sickness, morning sickness), carminative, digestive, anti-inflammatory, used in foods, beverages and confectionery.
- **Caution**: may add to the anti-platelet effect of anticoagulants in large amounts.

### Fenugreek

- **Source**: seeds of *Trigonella foenum-graecum*, family Fabaceae.
- **Constituents**: mucilage (**galactomannan**), steroidal saponins (diosgenin as the sapogenin), alkaloid **trigonelline**, amino acid **4-hydroxyisoleucine**, proteins, fixed oil.
- **Uses**: lowers blood glucose (fibre slows absorption; 4-hydroxyisoleucine increases insulin release), lowers cholesterol, galactagogue, spice, source of diosgenin.
- **Caution**: may increase the effect of antidiabetic drugs; maple-syrup odour of sweat and urine.

### Garlic

- **Source**: bulbs of *Allium sativum*, family Liliaceae (now often placed in Amaryllidaceae).
- **Constituents**: the odourless sulphur amino acid **alliin**; when the bulb is crushed, the enzyme **alliinase** converts it to **allicin**, which gives the smell and much of the activity; allicin breaks down to diallyl disulphide, ajoenes and other sulphides.
- **Uses**: lowers cholesterol and blood pressure modestly, reduces platelet aggregation, antimicrobial, antioxidant, food flavour.
- **Caution**: bleeding risk with anticoagulants; reduces blood levels of saquinavir (see 2.6).

### Honey

- **Source**: sugary substance made by honey bees, *Apis mellifera* and other *Apis* species (family Apidae), from the nectar of flowers.
- **Constituents**: invert sugar (fructose and glucose), a little sucrose, water, enzymes (invertase, diastase, glucose oxidase), organic acids, minerals, flavonoids and phenolic acids.
- **Uses**: nutritive sweetener, demulcent in coughs, wound and burn dressing (glucose oxidase forms hydrogen peroxide; high sugar and low pH stop microbes), vehicle (*anupana*) in Ayurveda.
- **Caution**: **not to be given to infants** under one year (risk of infant botulism); adds sugar load in diabetics; adulteration with sugar syrups is common.

### Amla (Indian gooseberry)

- **Source**: fruits of *Emblica officinalis* (*Phyllanthus emblica*), family Euphorbiaceae (now Phyllanthaceae).
- **Constituents**: one of the richest natural sources of **vitamin C** (ascorbic acid), hydrolysable tannins (emblicanins, gallic acid, ellagic acid), flavonoids, pectin.
- **Uses**: antioxidant, immunity booster, rasayana; ingredient of **Chyawanprash** and **Triphala**; hair tonic; lowers lipids and blood sugar in some studies; made into juices, candies and murabba.

### Ginseng

- **Source**: roots of *Panax ginseng* (Asian/Korean ginseng) and *Panax quinquefolius* (American ginseng), family Araliaceae.
- **Constituents**: triterpenoid saponins called **ginsenosides** (panaxosides), polysaccharides, volatile oil.
- **Uses**: **adaptogen** (increases resistance to stress), tonic for fatigue, improves mental and physical performance, mild blood-glucose lowering, immune modulation.
- **Caution**: insomnia, nervousness and high blood pressure with long use ("ginseng abuse syndrome"); interactions with warfarin, MAO inhibitors and antidiabetic drugs.

### Ashwagandha

- **Source**: roots of *Withania somnifera*, family Solanaceae.
- **Constituents**: steroidal lactones called **withanolides** (withaferin A, withanolide D), alkaloids (withanine, somniferine), sitoindosides, iron.
- **Uses**: rasayana and **adaptogen**, reduces stress and anxiety, improves sleep and strength, used for general debility; popular in powders, capsules and health drinks.
- **Caution**: may add to the effect of sedatives and thyroid medicines; avoided in pregnancy.

### Spirulina

- **Source**: dried biomass of the blue-green alga (cyanobacterium) *Spirulina platensis* and *S. maxima* (now *Arthrospira*), grown in alkaline water ponds.
- **Constituents**: very high **protein** content (more than half the dry weight, with all essential amino acids), the blue pigment **phycocyanin**, chlorophyll, carotenoids (beta-carotene), **gamma-linolenic acid**, B vitamins, iron.
- **Uses**: protein and micronutrient supplement in malnutrition, antioxidant and immune support, food colour (phycocyanin), feed for fish and poultry.
- **Caution**: products from contaminated ponds may carry **microcystins** (toxins from other algae) and heavy metals; its vitamin B12 is largely an inactive analogue, so it is not a reliable B12 source.

## 2.5 Herb–drug and herb–food interactions — introduction

An **interaction** occurs when the effect of one substance is changed by another taken at the same time. With herbs this is a real risk because: herbs contain many active compounds; patients take them without telling their doctor; products are not standardised; and many herbs affect drug-metabolising enzymes.

### Classification

| Type | Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pharmacokinetic** — changes how much drug reaches its site | | |
| Absorption | Binding, changed gut transit, changed P-glycoprotein | Fibre (isabgol) reduces absorption of drugs taken at the same time |
| Distribution | Displacement from plasma proteins | — |
| **Metabolism** (most important) | **Induction** or **inhibition** of cytochrome P450 (especially CYP3A4) and conjugating enzymes | St John's wort induces CYP3A4; piperine inhibits it |
| Excretion | Changed renal elimination or P-gp efflux | Liquorice changes potassium and fluid balance |
| **Pharmacodynamic** — changes the effect at the site | | |
| Additive / synergistic | Two agents with the same effect | Garlic + warfarin → bleeding; kava + benzodiazepines → sedation |
| Antagonistic | Opposing effects | Ginseng may reduce warfarin effect; ephedra opposes antihypertensives |

**Herb–food interactions** include foods that change drug or herb handling — the classic one being **grapefruit juice**, whose furanocoumarins inhibit intestinal CYP3A4 and raise levels of drugs such as some calcium-channel blockers and statins; and **tyramine-rich foods** (aged cheese, fermented foods) with MAO inhibitors. Herbs taken with food may also change food absorption — fibres slow sugar absorption, tannins reduce iron absorption.

```text
            Herb taken with drug
                    │
     ┌──────────────┴───────────────┐
 Pharmacokinetic                 Pharmacodynamic
 (drug level changes)           (drug effect changes)
     │                                │
 Induction of CYP/P-gp → ↓ level   Same effect → ↑ effect (additive)
 Inhibition of CYP/P-gp → ↑ level  Opposite effect → ↓ effect (antagonism)
```

## 2.6 Study of individual herbs: side effects and interactions

### Hypericum (St John's wort)

- **Source**: flowering tops of *Hypericum perforatum*, family Hypericaceae (Clusiaceae).
- **Constituents**: naphthodianthrones (**hypericin**, pseudohypericin), phloroglucinols (**hyperforin**), flavonoids.
- **Use**: mild to moderate depression.
- **Side effects**: **photosensitivity** (hypericin), gastrointestinal upset, restlessness.
- **Interactions**: hyperforin strongly **induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein**, which lowers the blood levels and effect of cyclosporine (risk of transplant rejection), digoxin, warfarin, **oral contraceptives** (breakthrough bleeding, pregnancy), HIV protease inhibitors (indinavir), theophylline and some anticancer drugs. With **SSRIs** and other serotonergic drugs it can cause **serotonin syndrome** (pharmacodynamic).

### Kava-kava

- **Source**: roots/rhizome of *Piper methysticum*, family Piperaceae (Pacific islands).
- **Constituents**: **kavalactones** (kavain, methysticin, yangonin).
- **Use**: anxiety, sleeplessness, ceremonial drink.
- **Side effects**: **liver damage** (hepatotoxicity — led to restrictions in several countries), skin scaling (kava dermopathy) with heavy use, drowsiness.
- **Interactions**: additive **CNS depression** with alcohol, benzodiazepines (alprazolam), barbiturates; may worsen parkinsonism and oppose levodopa; added risk of liver injury with other hepatotoxic drugs.

### Ginkgo biloba

- **Source**: leaves of *Ginkgo biloba*, family Ginkgoaceae; standardised extracts are used.
- **Constituents**: flavonol glycosides, terpene lactones (**ginkgolides A, B, C** and **bilobalide**).
- **Use**: memory and cognitive decline, peripheral circulation, tinnitus.
- **Side effects**: headache, gastrointestinal upset, allergic skin reactions; seeds contain a neurotoxin (ginkgotoxin) that can cause seizures.
- **Interactions**: ginkgolide B antagonises **platelet-activating factor**, so with **warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel or NSAIDs** there is a risk of bleeding; avoid before surgery; may lower the seizure threshold with drugs such as anticonvulsants.

### Ginseng

- **Side effects**: insomnia, nervousness, headache, raised blood pressure, oestrogen-like effects (breast tenderness), hypoglycaemia.
- **Interactions**: may **reduce the effect of warfarin** (lowered INR reported); with **MAO inhibitors** (phenelzine) — headache, tremor, mania; with **insulin and oral antidiabetics** — added fall in blood glucose; with stimulants — overstimulation.

### Garlic

- **Side effects**: bad breath and body odour, heartburn, flatulence, contact dermatitis.
- **Interactions**: antiplatelet effect → **bleeding** with warfarin, aspirin and other anticoagulants (stop before surgery); **reduces blood levels of saquinavir** (an HIV protease inhibitor), probably by inducing intestinal CYP3A4/P-gp; additive fall in blood glucose with antidiabetic drugs.

### Pepper

- **Source**: dried unripe fruits of *Piper nigrum* (black pepper) and *Piper longum* (long pepper), family Piperaceae.
- **Constituent**: the alkaloid **piperine**.
- **Side effects**: gastric irritation in large amounts.
- **Interactions**: piperine **inhibits CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein and glucuronidation**, and increases blood flow in the gut, so it **raises the bioavailability** of many drugs — phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, rifampicin, nevirapine. This "**bioenhancer**" effect is used in the Ayurvedic combination **Trikatu** (black pepper, long pepper, ginger) and in some modern formulations (piperine with curcumin), but it can also push narrow-therapeutic-index drugs into toxic levels.

### Ephedra (Ma huang)

- **Source**: stems of *Ephedra sinica* and other *Ephedra* species, family Ephedraceae.
- **Constituents**: **ephedrine** and pseudoephedrine (sympathomimetic amines).
- **Use**: asthma, nasal congestion; widely misused in weight-loss and sports products.
- **Side effects**: hypertension, palpitations, arrhythmias, stroke, seizures, insomnia, anxiety; deaths have been reported, and the US FDA banned dietary supplements containing ephedra alkaloids.
- **Interactions**: with **MAO inhibitors** — hypertensive crisis; with **caffeine** and other stimulants — added cardiovascular toxicity; with **cardiac glycosides** and halogenated anaesthetics (halothane) — arrhythmias; opposes antihypertensive drugs; with ergot alkaloids or oxytocin — severe hypertension.

### Quick interaction table

| Herb | Key constituent | Main interaction | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| St John's wort | Hyperforin | CYP3A4 and P-gp induction | ↓ cyclosporine, digoxin, OCs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs |
| Kava-kava | Kavalactones | Additive CNS depression; liver toxicity | Sedation with benzodiazepines, alcohol |
| Ginkgo | Ginkgolide B | PAF antagonism | Bleeding with anticoagulants |
| Ginseng | Ginsenosides | Pharmacodynamic | ↓ warfarin effect; mania with MAOIs; hypoglycaemia |
| Garlic | Allicin, ajoene | Antiplatelet; CYP3A4 induction | Bleeding; ↓ saquinavir |
| Pepper | Piperine | CYP3A4, P-gp inhibition | ↑ phenytoin, theophylline, propranolol |
| Ephedra | Ephedrine | Sympathomimetic | Hypertensive crisis with MAOIs; arrhythmia |

**Role of the pharmacist**: always ask about herbal and supplement use when dispensing, especially with narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (warfarin, digoxin, cyclosporine, phenytoin, theophylline), before surgery, in pregnancy and in the elderly; report suspected interactions through pharmacovigilance.

## Remember

- Nutraceutical = food or food part with medical benefit (DeFelice, 1989); in India regulated by FSSAI as food.
- Types: dietary supplements, functional foods, herbal products, probiotics/prebiotics/synbiotics.
- Diabetes: fenugreek, fibre, cinnamon; CVS: omega-3, garlic, phytosterols, fibre; cancer: lycopene, curcumin, EGCG, sulforaphane; IBS/GI: probiotics, psyllium, peppermint oil.
- Alfalfa — *Medicago sativa* (L-canavanine); chicory — inulin; ginger — gingerols/shogaols; fenugreek — galactomannan, 4-hydroxyisoleucine, diosgenin; garlic — alliin → allicin by alliinase; honey — invert sugar, not for infants; amla — vitamin C, emblicanins; ginseng — ginsenosides, adaptogen; ashwagandha — withanolides; spirulina — protein, phycocyanin, GLA.
- Interactions: pharmacokinetic (CYP3A4/P-gp induction or inhibition) and pharmacodynamic (additive or antagonistic).
- Hypericum induces CYP3A4 (↓ drug levels); piperine inhibits it (↑ drug levels, Trikatu bioenhancer).
- Ginkgo and garlic → bleeding with anticoagulants; kava → liver injury and sedation; ephedra → hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
- Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 — the classic food–drug interaction.

# Unit 3: Herbal cosmetics, herbal excipients and herbal formulations

Plants give the cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries much more than active drugs. Oils, waxes, gums, colours, perfumes and antioxidants of plant origin go into creams, shampoos and toothpastes; starches, gums and sugars go into tablets and syrups as excipients. This unit covers these raw materials, how they are used in skin, hair and oral products, the role of natural excipients, and how herbal extracts are made into conventional dosage forms (syrups, mixtures, tablets) and into a novel form, the phytosome.

## 3.1 Herbal cosmetics — introduction

A **cosmetic** is a product meant to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on the body to cleanse, beautify, make attractive or change the appearance, without affecting the body's structure or function. A **herbal cosmetic** uses ingredients of plant origin — extracts, oils, waxes, gums, colours or perfumes — either as the base or as the active part. In India cosmetics are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Cosmetics Rules.

Why herbal cosmetics are popular: consumer belief that natural is mild and safe, fewer synthetic chemicals, traditional use (turmeric, sandalwood, henna, neem, amla), and multiple benefits in one ingredient (aloe moisturises and soothes). They still need preservatives, stability testing and patch testing, because plant materials can cause allergy and grow microbes.

## 3.2 Raw materials of herbal origin

### Fixed oils

Fixed oils are esters of glycerol with fatty acids (triglycerides). They soften the skin (emollients), form a film that reduces water loss, and act as the oily phase of creams and lotions.

| Oil | Source and family | Cosmetic use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coconut oil | Kernel of *Cocos nucifera*, Arecaceae | Hair oil, soaps (lauric acid gives good lather), creams |
| Olive oil | Fruit of *Olea europaea*, Oleaceae | Emollient in creams, massage oils, baby products |
| Almond oil | Seeds of *Prunus amygdalus*, Rosaceae | Emollient, skin and baby oils, under-eye creams |
| Castor oil | Seeds of *Ricinus communis*, Euphorbiaceae | Lipsticks (gloss, dissolves dyes), hair oils |
| Sesame (til) oil | Seeds of *Sesamum indicum*, Pedaliaceae | Massage oils, base for Ayurvedic oils |
| Sunflower, groundnut, jojoba* | — | Skin creams, hair conditioners |

*Jojoba "oil" from *Simmondsia chinensis* is really a **liquid wax**, very stable and close to skin sebum.

### Waxes

Waxes are esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain alcohols. They give body, hardness and gloss, and raise the melting point of sticks and creams.

| Wax | Source | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Beeswax** | Honeycomb of *Apis* species | Cold creams (with borax forms an emulsifier), lipsticks, lip balms |
| **Carnauba wax** | Leaves of the palm *Copernicia cerifera* (*C. prunifera*) | Hardest natural wax; gives gloss and stiffness to lipsticks, mascara; tablet polishing |
| **Candelilla wax** | Stems of *Euphorbia cerifera* | Lipsticks, a substitute for beeswax |
| Jojoba wax | Seeds of *Simmondsia chinensis* | Skin and hair products |
| Lanolin (wool fat)* | Sheep wool | Emollient — animal origin, often grouped here |

### Gums and mucilages

Gums are polysaccharides that swell or dissolve in water to form viscous solutions or gels. In cosmetics they thicken lotions and gels, stabilise emulsions and form films.

- **Acacia** (gum arabic) — *Acacia senegal*, Fabaceae: emulsifier, film former in face masks.
- **Tragacanth** — *Astragalus gummifer*, Fabaceae: thickener for lotions and gels, hair-setting lotions.
- **Karaya** — *Sterculia urens*, Sterculiaceae (Malvaceae): denture adhesives, hair-setting.
- **Guar gum** — seed endosperm of *Cyamopsis tetragonolobus*, Fabaceae: thickener, conditioning agent (as guar derivatives) in shampoos.
- **Xanthan gum** — produced by the bacterium *Xanthomonas campestris*: stable thickener over wide pH.
- **Agar, alginates, carrageenan** — from seaweeds: gels and thickeners.
- **Aloe gel** — *Aloe vera* (*A. barbadensis*), Asphodelaceae/Liliaceae: soothing, moisturising.

### Colours

| Colour | Source and pigment | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Orange-red (hair, nails) | **Henna** — leaves of *Lawsonia inermis*, Lythraceae; **lawsone** (a naphthoquinone) binds keratin | Hair dye, mehendi |
| Yellow | **Turmeric** — *Curcuma longa*, Zingiberaceae; **curcumin** | Creams, fairness and anti-acne products |
| Orange-yellow | **Annatto** — seeds of *Bixa orellana*; **bixin** (carotenoid) | Lipsticks, soaps |
| Yellow | **Saffron** — stigmas of *Crocus sativus*, Iridaceae; **crocin** | Premium creams |
| Red-violet | **Beetroot** — *Beta vulgaris*; **betanin** | Lip and cheek tints |
| Blue / black | **Indigo** — *Indigofera tinctoria*; indigotin (with henna for black hair) | Hair dyes |
| Green | **Chlorophyll** (and copper chlorophyllin) | Soaps, toothpastes |
| Red | Carmine from cochineal insect (animal origin) | Lipsticks |
| Red | Red sandalwood — *Pterocarpus santalinus*; santalins | Face packs |

### Perfumes

Natural perfumes are mostly **volatile oils** obtained by steam distillation, expression, solvent extraction or enfleurage.

| Perfume | Source | Main constituents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rose oil | Petals of *Rosa damascena*, Rosaceae | Geraniol, citronellol, phenylethyl alcohol |
| Jasmine | Flowers of *Jasminum grandiflorum*, Oleaceae (absolute) | Benzyl acetate, jasmone |
| Sandalwood oil | Heartwood of *Santalum album*, Santalaceae | Santalols |
| Lavender oil | *Lavandula angustifolia*, Lamiaceae | Linalool, linalyl acetate |
| Vetiver (khus) | Roots of *Vetiveria zizanioides*, Poaceae | Vetiverols — fixative |
| Lemongrass | *Cymbopogon flexuosus*, Poaceae | Citral |
| Patchouli | *Pogostemon cablin*, Lamiaceae | Patchouli alcohol — fixative |

### Protective agents

Protective agents shield the skin from sun, water loss, irritation and microbes:

- **Sun protection**: extracts rich in polyphenols and flavonoids (green tea, aloe, turmeric) give some antioxidant and UV-protective support; vegetable oils with natural tocopherols. Mineral filters such as zinc oxide are often combined.
- **Moisturisers and humectants**: aloe gel, honey, glycerin of vegetable origin.
- **Barrier agents**: vegetable butters (cocoa butter from *Theobroma cacao*, shea butter from *Vitellaria paradoxa*), waxes.
- **Soothing and healing agents**: aloe, calendula, chamomile, liquorice, neem (antibacterial).

### Bleaching (skin-lightening) agents

These reduce dark spots and uneven pigment by blocking the enzyme **tyrosinase**, which makes melanin, or by gentle exfoliation:

- **Liquorice** root extract (*Glycyrrhiza glabra*) — glabridin.
- **Arbutin** — from bearberry (*Arctostaphylos uva-ursi*) leaves.
- **Kojic acid** — from fungi (*Aspergillus*) fermentation.
- **Lemon juice** — citric acid and vitamin C; **papaya** (papain) and **pineapple** (bromelain) — enzymatic exfoliation.
- **Turmeric** (curcumin), **saffron**, **mulberry** extract, **vitamin C** derivatives.

### Antioxidants

Antioxidants stop oils going rancid and protect skin from free radicals.

- **Tocopherols** (vitamin E) — wheat germ, sunflower, soybean oils.
- **Ascorbic acid** (vitamin C) — amla, citrus.
- **Rosemary extract** — carnosic acid, carnosol, rosmarinic acid.
- **Green tea** — catechins (EGCG).
- **Grape seed** — proanthocyanidins; **curcumin**; **sesamol** from sesame oil.

## 3.3 Herbal products: skin care, hair care and oral hygiene

### Skin care

| Product | Herbal ingredients and their role |
| --- | --- |
| Cold cream / vanishing cream | Beeswax, almond or olive oil (base); aloe, rose water, saffron, turmeric (actives) |
| Face packs | Multani mitti with sandalwood, turmeric, neem, orange peel |
| Anti-acne products | Neem, tulsi, turmeric, tea tree oil (antibacterial, anti-inflammatory) |
| Moisturisers | Aloe gel, cocoa/shea butter, honey, glycerin |
| Sunscreen and anti-ageing | Green tea, aloe, vitamin E, grape seed |
| Soaps | Coconut, palm and castor oils saponified; neem, sandalwood, turmeric |

### Hair care

| Product | Herbal ingredients and their role |
| --- | --- |
| Herbal shampoo | **Shikakai** (*Acacia concinna*) pods and **reetha** (soapnut, *Sapindus mukorossi*) — natural saponins that lather and cleanse; amla, hibiscus |
| Hair oil | Coconut or sesame oil base with amla, **bhringraj** (*Eclipta alba*), brahmi, hibiscus, neem |
| Hair dye | Henna (lawsone), indigo, catechu, amla |
| Anti-dandruff | Neem, tea tree oil, fenugreek, lemon |
| Conditioner | Aloe, hibiscus mucilage, guar derivatives |

### Oral hygiene

| Product | Herbal ingredients and their role |
| --- | --- |
| Herbal toothpaste / tooth powder | **Neem** (antibacterial), **babool** (*Acacia arabica*, astringent), **clove oil** (eugenol — analgesic, antiseptic), **peppermint** (menthol — flavour and cooling), meswak (*Salvadora persica*), turmeric, bakul, triphala |
| Mouthwash | Peppermint, clove, eucalyptus, thyme (thymol), tulsi, liquorice |
| Chewing sticks (datun) | Neem and babool twigs, miswak |

In formulation, abrasives (calcium carbonate), humectants (sorbitol, glycerin), thickeners (gums), foaming agents and sweeteners are added to the herbal actives.

## 3.4 Herbal excipients

An **excipient** is any substance other than the active ingredient that is added to a dosage form to help in manufacture, protect the product, or improve patient acceptance, release or absorption.

### Significance of natural excipients

Advantages:

- **Biocompatible and non-toxic**; many are eaten as food.
- **Biodegradable** and eco-friendly.
- **Cheap and widely available**, renewable.
- Can be **chemically modified** (pregelatinised starch, sodium starch glycolate, carboxymethyl derivatives) to improve properties.
- Patient acceptance and suitability for "natural" products.

Disadvantages:

- **Batch-to-batch variation** with source, season and processing.
- **Microbial contamination** — need tight limits.
- **Uncontrolled hydration and viscosity changes** on storage.
- Possible **heavy-metal and pesticide** contamination.
- Slow, variable supply and the need for standardisation.

### Classes and examples

| Function | Herbal examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Colorants** | Curcumin, chlorophyll, caramel, carotenoids (beta-carotene, annatto), anthocyanins, beetroot red | Improve appearance and identification; less stable to light and pH than synthetic dyes |
| **Sweeteners** | Sucrose (sugarcane, beet), honey, glucose (from starch), **stevioside/rebaudioside** (*Stevia rebaudiana* leaves, many times sweeter than sugar, non-caloric), **glycyrrhizin** (liquorice), **thaumatin** (protein from *Thaumatococcus daniellii* fruit), **mogrosides** (monk fruit), sorbitol and mannitol (from glucose/mannose) | Natural non-caloric sweeteners suit diabetics |
| **Binders** | Acacia, tragacanth, **starch paste**, pregelatinised starch, gelatin (animal), alginates, guar gum, cellulose derivatives | Hold tablet granules together |
| **Diluents (fillers)** | Starch (maize, potato, rice), **microcrystalline cellulose** (from wood pulp), lactose (from milk), sucrose, mannitol, calcium carbonate | Give bulk to small-dose tablets |
| **Viscosity builders** | Acacia, tragacanth, guar, xanthan, sodium alginate, pectin, agar, carrageenan, methylcellulose | Thicken liquids, suspend particles, stabilise emulsions |
| **Disintegrants** | Starch, **sodium starch glycolate**, alginic acid, MCC, agar, guar gum, isabgol husk | Swell in water and break the tablet |
| **Flavours and perfumes** | Peppermint, spearmint, lemon, orange, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, vanilla, anise oils | Mask taste, improve acceptance |
| Others | Lubricants (vegetable stearates, talc), coating agents (shellac — insect resin; zein — maize protein), gelling agents (pectin, agar) | — |

A natural excipient must be **standardised** like any raw material: identity, moisture, ash, swelling index, viscosity, pH, particle size, microbial limits and heavy metals.

## 3.5 Herbal formulations

Herbal extracts are difficult to formulate: they are mixtures, often coloured, bitter or hygroscopic, may be sticky and may contain constituents that degrade. Steps common to all formulations:

1. **Prepare and standardise the extract** — fixed solvent, ratio of drug to extract (DER), marker content, solvent residue, microbial and heavy-metal limits.
2. **Pre-formulation** — solubility, hygroscopicity, stability to heat, light and pH, compatibility with excipients.
3. **Formulation and process** design.
4. **Evaluation** as per pharmacopoeia, plus marker assay and fingerprint.
5. **Stability testing** in the final pack.

### Herbal syrups

A syrup is a concentrated, viscous aqueous solution of sugar (or sugar substitute) containing the extract or a decoction. Example: cough syrups with vasaka, tulsi, mulethi; tonic syrups with ashwagandha.

**Method**: dissolve sucrose in purified water with heat (simple syrup) → cool → add the aqueous or hydroalcoholic extract (or fluid extract) gradually with stirring → add preservatives (methyl/propyl paraben, sodium benzoate), flavour and colour → make up to volume → filter → fill into clean amber bottles.

**Evaluation**: appearance and clarity, pH, specific gravity, viscosity, sugar content, marker assay, alcohol content (if any), microbial limit, preservative efficacy, fill volume, stability.

### Herbal mixtures

A mixture is a liquid oral preparation in which the drugs are dissolved or **suspended** in an aqueous vehicle. Herbal mixtures often contain insoluble powders or extracts that need a suspending agent.

**Method**: wet the powder or extract with a little vehicle → add a suspending agent (tragacanth, acacia, xanthan or sodium CMC) → add the rest of the vehicle, preservative and flavour → homogenise → make up to volume → label "Shake well before use".

**Evaluation**: sedimentation volume (F = Hu/Ho, ratio of settled-sediment height to original height), ease of redispersion, viscosity, pH, particle size, marker assay, microbial limits.

### Herbal tablets

**Method** (wet granulation, the usual route for extracts):

```text
Standardised dry extract + diluent (MCC, starch) + disintegrant
          │ mix
          ▼
Granulate with binder (starch paste, PVP, acacia)  →  sieve wet mass
          │
          ▼
Dry granules (controlled temperature)  →  sieve dry granules
          │
          ▼
Add lubricant and glidant (magnesium stearate, talc)  →  compress
          │
          ▼
(Film-coat to mask taste, odour and protect from moisture)
```

Problems with extracts: **hygroscopic, sticky** extracts cause picking and sticking — use adsorbents (colloidal silica), dry granulation or coating; **high dose** of extract makes large tablets — use concentrated extracts.

**Evaluation (pharmacopoeial)**: appearance, uniformity of weight, hardness, friability, disintegration time, dissolution (where marker can be measured), content of marker, moisture, microbial limits.

## 3.6 Novel dosage forms — phytosomes

Many plant actives, especially **polyphenols and flavonoids**, are water-soluble but too polar to cross the lipid membranes of the gut, and others are poorly soluble in water. Both give poor oral bioavailability. **Phytosomes** solve this.

**Definition**: a phytosome is a **complex between a natural active constituent and a phospholipid**, usually **phosphatidylcholine** from soy lecithin, in which the active is bonded to the polar head of the phospholipid. The term and the technology were developed by the Italian company **Indena**.

```text
       Phosphatidylcholine molecule
   Polar head (choline-phosphate) ── H-bonds ── Polyphenol / flavonoid
            │
   Two fatty-acid tails (lipophilic)  → wrap the complex, make it
                                        compatible with cell membranes
```

**Preparation**: the phospholipid and the active (or extract) are reacted in a fixed molar ratio (often 1:1 or 2:1) in an aprotic solvent such as dioxane or acetone (or by modern methods like solvent evaporation, anti-solvent precipitation or freeze-drying); the complex is recovered by precipitation with a non-solvent or by drying.

**Phytosome versus liposome**

| Feature | Phytosome | Liposome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Binding | Active is chemically bonded (H-bonds) to phospholipid — part of the membrane | Active is enclosed in the aqueous core or bilayer, not bonded |
| Phospholipid : active | Low, defined molar ratio | Large excess of phospholipid |
| Stability | Better; less leakage | Leakage of contents possible |
| Bioavailability gain | Large, for polar polyphenols | Variable |

**Advantages**: much better absorption and bioavailability of polar polyphenols; lower dose needed; phosphatidylcholine itself is hepatoprotective; good skin penetration in cosmetics; stable complex.

**Examples**: silybin phytosome (from milk thistle, *Silybum marianum*), ginkgo phytosome, green tea (EGCG) phytosome, curcumin phytosome, grape seed phytosome, ginseng phytosome, hawthorn phytosome.

**Characterisation**: complex formation by IR, NMR, DSC and X-ray diffraction; particle size and zeta potential; solubility and partition coefficient; drug content; in vitro release and in vivo bioavailability.

Other novel herbal delivery systems often mentioned: liposomes, niosomes, ethosomes (skin), nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles, microspheres, nanoemulsions and self-emulsifying systems — all aim to improve solubility, absorption, stability and targeting of herbal actives.

## Remember

- Herbal cosmetic raw materials: fixed oils (coconut, olive, almond, castor), waxes (beeswax, carnauba, candelilla; jojoba is a liquid wax), gums (acacia, tragacanth, karaya, guar, xanthan), colours (lawsone, curcumin, bixin, crocin, betanin, indigo, chlorophyll), perfumes (rose, jasmine, sandalwood, lavender, vetiver).
- Bleaching agents block tyrosinase: liquorice (glabridin), arbutin, kojic acid, vitamin C.
- Antioxidants: tocopherols, ascorbic acid, rosemary (carnosic acid), green tea catechins.
- Hair: shikakai and reetha (saponins), amla, bhringraj, henna. Oral: neem, babool, clove (eugenol), peppermint (menthol), miswak.
- Natural excipients: biocompatible, cheap, biodegradable — but variable and microbe-prone; must be standardised.
- Sweeteners: stevioside, glycyrrhizin, thaumatin, mogrosides; disintegrants: starch, sodium starch glycolate, alginic acid.
- Syrups, mixtures (sedimentation volume) and tablets (wet granulation; sticky extracts need adsorbents) are evaluated as per pharmacopoeia plus marker assay.
- Phytosome = phosphatidylcholine–polyphenol complex (Indena); better bioavailability than free extract; differs from liposome in bonding and ratio; silybin phytosome is the classic example.
